# Ray Traversal Schemes

Also called: Accumulate Projection, Depth Projection, Max Intensity Projection, Ray Traversal -Accumulate

## Overview
Ray traversal schemes define the aggregation logic applied to sample values along a ray to produce a final pixel color, ranging from simple scalar projections to full volumetric [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) [S1, S2, S3, unofficial]. Unlike standard [front-to-back volume ray casting](#4324-front-to-back-volume-ray-casting-with-hsv-shading-and-sos-at.md) which integrates opacity and color to simulate light transport, these schemes often prioritize specific data features (such as maximum intensity or average density) or simplified accumulation models [S2, S3, unofficial]. They differ from [Ray Marching and Discretization](2788-ray-marching-and-discretization.md) by focusing on the compositing/aggregation operator rather than the [step-size selection](#2331-step-size-selection.md), and from [Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering](4980-monte-carlo-path-tracing-for-volume-rendering.md) by using deterministic integration paths [S2, S3, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the discretized ray segment $[t_{start}, t_{end}]$ defined in the parent article. For each sample $i$ along the ray, a scalar value $d_i$ (intensity) and optionally an opacity $\alpha_i$ are obtained via sampling and classification [S1, S2, S3, unofficial]. The core distinction lies in the reduction function $R$ that maps the sequence of samples $\{(d_i, \alpha_i)\}$ to a single pixel result. The parent article's compositing equation is a specific instance (Accumulate) of these schemes [S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Intensity Projection
Projects the raw scalar value of a single sample or the final sample onto the pixel. It is rarely used in isolation for visualization as it lacks depth cues, serving primarily as a baseline for other schemes [S1, S2, unofficial].

### Max Intensity Projection (MIP)
Projects the maximum scalar value encountered along the ray. It is used to visualize high-intensity structures, such as blood vessels in Magnetic Resonance Angiography, by ignoring lower-intensity background tissue [S2, S3, unofficial].

### Average Projection
Averages the scalar values along the ray. It produces an X-ray-like picture where dense structures appear brighter or darker depending on the transfer function, effectively integrating density [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].

### Accumulate Projection
Accumulates opacity while compositing colors to make transparent layers visible. This is the standard volumetric compositing approach described in the parent article, often attributed to Levoy (1988) [S2, S3, unofficial]. It handles transparency and depth simultaneously.

### First Projection
Extracts the first sample that meets a specific criterion (e.g., threshold crossing). It is used to extract iso-surfaces or the first intersection with a structure [S1, S2, unofficial].

### Depth Projection
Records the distance $t$ or index $i$ of the sample that determined the final pixel value (e.g., the sample with max intensity in [MIP](#6635-fast-maximum-intensity-projection-mip.md)). It is used for depth mapping or auxiliary buffers [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].

## Background
The classification of these schemes appears in educational materials on [Direct Volume Rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) (DVR) and [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) pipelines [S1, S2, S3, unofficial]. The "Accumulate" scheme is explicitly linked to Levoy (1988) in these sources [S2, S3, unofficial]. The "Max" scheme is noted for its application in Magnetic Resonance Angiography [S2, S3, unofficial]. The "First" scheme is associated with iso-surface extraction techniques [S1, unofficial].
